_note: SYNTHETIC - classification guide written by AI in our own words for a hackathon demo. Not real patient data. Not clinically validated.

A.name: Life-threatening
A.response: Nearest ambulance now, lights and sirens. Operator gives first aid instructions (CPR, EpiPen, recovery position) while waiting.

B.name: Urgent, potentially serious
B.response: Ambulance as soon as possible, sirens at crew's discretion. Re-check symptoms every few minutes and raise to A if they worsen.

C.name: Needs assessment, stable now
C.response: Ambulance without lights, or other transport to emergency care. Caller told to call back if worse.

D.name: Not urgent
D.response: No ambulance. Advice and referral to 1177 / health centre / own transport.

E.name: Other help
E.response: No medical response needed now. Police, social services, poison info or other agency.

rules: AI suggests, the human operator decides. AI may RAISE urgency on its own; only a human can LOWER it.
Every red flag shown to the operator must carry the exact quote from the call that triggered it.
When information is missing, the category is uncertain: show the missing question instead of guessing low.
If several categories fit, the most urgent one sets the urgency.

categories.name: Chest pain / suspected heart attack

A: chest pain or pressure with sweating, nausea, shortness of breath, pallor or fainting
pain spreading to arm, jaw, neck or back
known heart disease and pain not like usual / not helped by own nitro
atypical presentation in women, elderly or diabetics: nausea, jaw/upper back pain, unusual fatigue, 'feels like flu'
B: chest pain now gone (< 12 h) in someone over 30
chest pain with palpitations but otherwise stable
C: pain clearly linked to movement or pressing on the chest, young and otherwise healthy
D: long-standing, known, unchanged pain with a clear non-cardiac cause

red_flags: like an elephant on my chest
key_questions: Is the person awake and breathing normally?
When did the pain start?
Where is the pain and does it spread (arm, jaw, back)?
Sweating, nausea, short of breath?
Any heart disease, previous heart attack, diabetes?
Age?
Do they have nitroglycerin or aspirin, and are they allergic to aspirin?
operator_instructions: Sit the person down, loosen clothing
Aspirin 300 mg chewed if not allergic (per local protocol)
Have someone fetch nearest AED
Call back immediately if they collapse

categories.name: Breathing difficulty

A: can only say a few words between breaths
blue or grey lips/face
drowsy, confused or exhausted
noisy breathing / stridor, choking
breathing difficulty with chest pain
B: clearly short of breath but can talk in sentences
known asthma/COPD, own medication not helping
fever plus breathing difficulty in elderly
C: mild breathlessness on exertion only, stable, normal colour

key_questions: Can they speak full sentences?
What colour are lips and face?
Awake and alert?
Known asthma, COPD, heart failure?
Have they used their inhaler/home oxygen, did it help?
Did it start suddenly (choking, allergy)?
Chest pain or fever?
operator_instructions: Let them sit upright, leaning forward
Use own inhaler / home oxygen as prescribed
Open windows, calm the person

categories.name: Allergic reaction / anaphylaxis

A: swelling of lips, tongue or throat
breathing difficulty, wheezing, hoarse voice
faintness, collapse, pale and clammy
known severe allergy plus exposure plus any symptom beyond skin
B: widespread hives with vomiting or stomach pain
rapidly spreading rash after known allergen
C: local swelling (e.g. insect sting) without general symptoms
D: mild itchy rash, hours old, no other symptoms, stable

red_flags: peanut / nuts / bee sting + known allergy
key_questions: What were they exposed to and when?
Swelling of lips, tongue or throat?
Any breathing difficulty or change in voice?
Known allergy? Do they carry an EpiPen?
Has the EpiPen been used, and when?
Feeling faint or dizzy?
operator_instructions: Use the EpiPen now in outer thigh if available
Lie down with legs raised, or sit if breathing is hard
Second EpiPen after 5-15 min if no improvement

categories.name: Unconscious / not breathing normally (possible cardiac arrest)

A: does not respond and is not breathing normally (gasping, snoring, irregular = NOT normal)
unconscious, breathing status unknown
unconscious after trauma or with suspected overdose
B: was unconscious briefly, now awake but not fully alert
C: short faint, now fully recovered, young, clear cause (e.g. blood test)

red_flags: a bit sleepy (when caller cannot wake them)
key_questions: Is the person awake? Shout and shake their shoulders.
Are they breathing normally? Look for 10 seconds.
Is there an AED nearby?
What happened just before?
Exact address and door code?
categories.ambulance: Yes, A. Start telephone CPR immediately if not breathing normally.
operator_instructions: Telephone CPR: 30 compressions, hard and fast, middle of chest
Send someone for the nearest AED
If breathing normally: recovery position, keep checking

categories.name: Stroke symptoms

A: sudden face drooping, arm weakness or speech difficulty with onset < 24 h or unknown
sudden severe headache ('worst ever')
stroke symptoms plus reduced consciousness
B: symptoms that came and went within the last 24 h (TIA)

red_flags: fell and can't get up, one side weak
key_questions: When exactly were they last seen well? (time is brain)
Face: does one side droop when they smile?
Arms: can they lift both and hold them up?
Speech: can they repeat a simple sentence?
Blood thinners? Diabetes (check sugar)?
Awake?
operator_instructions: Note the time last seen well
Do not give food, drink or medicine
Gather list of medications

categories.name: Seizure / convulsions

A: seizure still going on (> 5 min) or repeated without waking between
not breathing normally after seizure
seizure in pregnancy, after head injury, or in diabetic
first-ever seizure in adult with headache/fever
B: first seizure, now stopped, child with fever
known epilepsy but seizure unlike usual or injury
C: known epilepsy, typical short seizure, now fully awake

key_questions: Is the seizure still going on? When did it start?
Breathing and colour?
First ever? Known epilepsy?
Fever, head injury, diabetes, pregnancy, drugs?
Age? Child's weight?
Has rescue medicine been given?
operator_instructions: Do not hold them down, nothing in mouth
Move hard objects away, protect head
Time the seizure
Recovery position when it stops

categories.name: Traffic collision / trauma

A: anyone unconscious, not breathing normally, or major bleeding
trapped in vehicle
pedestrian/cyclist hit by car at speed, thrown or run over
high-energy: rollover, ejection, fatality in same vehicle
B: neck/back pain after collision, chest or abdominal pain
head injury with vomiting or confusion
suspected fracture of thigh or pelvis

key_questions: Exact location / nearest junction?
How many people injured, how many vehicles?
Is anyone unconscious or not breathing normally?
Major bleeding?
Anyone trapped?
Is the scene safe (traffic, fire, fuel)?
Approximate speed?
categories.ambulance: Yes for A and B; police and rescue service for trapped, fire or blocked road.
operator_instructions: Keep yourself safe, warning triangle / hazard lights
Do not move the injured unless danger
Press hard on bleeding
Keep them warm, talk to them

categories.name: Mental health crisis / suicide risk

A: has taken an overdose or harmed themselves
has a plan AND means available right now
acute danger to self or others, weapon
B: active suicidal thoughts with plan but no immediate means
severe agitation, psychosis, not safe alone
C: suicidal thoughts without plan, someone can stay with them
D: distress, no suicidal thoughts, wants to talk (refer to crisis line / psychiatric emergency)
E: third party worried, no contact with person (police welfare check)

red_flags: took my pills / took more than usual
key_questions: Are you thinking of killing yourself? (ask directly)
Have you done anything to hurt yourself today? Taken anything?
What and how much, and when?
Do you have a plan, and the means with you now?
Is anyone with you?
Exact address?
categories.ambulance: Yes for A; A/B also police support for scene safety and psychiatric team where available.
operator_instructions: Stay on the line, calm voice
Ask directly about suicide; it does not increase risk
Remove means if safe
Unlock the door if able
